Tiny C++ Book

A very small book used to test the lesson maker. Read the text, run the code.

Chapter 1 Saying Hello

Every C++ program starts in a job called main. The computer runs the lines inside it, one after another. Printing words on the screen is done with cout.

A semicolon ends each line that does something. Forgetting it is the most common mistake for a new programmer.

Here is the smallest useful program.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, reader!" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Run it and you will see the greeting appear.

Chapter 2 Boxes for Numbers

A variable is a named box that holds a value. The type in front of the name says what kind of value fits inside.

2.1 Whole numbers

An int holds whole numbers. You can print it by putting its name after the output arrows.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int apples = 3;
    int pears = 4;
    int total = apples + pears;
    std::cout << "Total fruit: " << total << "\n";
    return 0;
}

2.2 Pieces of a program

Often a book shows only the interesting lines. These lines are not a whole program, but they can still be run.

int width = 6;
int height = 7;
std::cout << "Area: " << width * height << "\n";

Chapter 3 Doing Things Again

A loop repeats lines. The for loop counts for you, which saves a lot of typing.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i) {
        std::cout << "Count " << i << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Here is the very same loop once more, as if the book repeated itself. The lesson maker should notice and make lessons for it only once.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i) {
        std::cout << "Count " << i << "
";
    }
    return 0;
}

This one asks the person for a number, so the lesson maker gives it a simple answer.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;
    std::cout << "Double is " << n * 2 << "\n";
    return 0;
}
